etymology: From Latin foedus (covenant). The Reformed-confessional doctrine that Adam and Christ each acted as the covenant head (federal representative) of those they represent — Adam of all mankind in the covenant of works, Christ of the elect in the covenant of grace. Romans 5:12-21; 1 Corinthians 15:22, 45-49.
biblical_def: From Latin foedus (covenant); the Reformed-confessional doctrine that Adam and Christ each acted as the covenant head, or federal representative, of those they represent. The doctrine is the structural backbone of Reformed covenant theology and soteriology. Adam was the federal head of all mankind in the covenant of works: when Adam sinned, he sinned not merely as a private individual but as the representative of the whole human race, so that his guilt and corruption are imputed to and inherited by all his natural descendants (Romans 5:12, by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned; Romans 5:18-19, by the offence of one judgment came upon all men to condemnation... by one man's disobedience many were made sinners). Christ is the federal head of the elect in the covenant of grace: as the last Adam (1 Corinthians 15:45) and the second man (1 Corinthians 15:47), Christ's perfect obedience and atoning death are imputed to and received by all whom He represents, so that by the righteousness of one the free gift came upon all men unto justification of life... by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous (Romans 5:18-19). The doctrine is grounded in the Adam-Christ parallel that Paul develops at length (Romans 5:12-21; 1 Corinthians 15:22, as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds federal headship as the substantive structure of the gospel: we are condemned in Adam our first federal head and justified in Christ our second federal head; the imputation of Adam's sin and the imputation of Christ's righteousness are the two pillars of Reformed soteriology.
webster_summary: Reformed-confessional doctrine that Adam and Christ each acted as covenant head (federal representative) — Adam of all mankind in the covenant of works, Christ of the elect in the covenant of grace; the Adam-Christ parallel (Romans 5:12-21; 1 Corinthians 15:22, 45-49).
webster_full: FEDERAL HEADSHIP (THEOLOGY), n. phr. (covenant theology; Latin foedus, covenant) Adam and Christ each acted as the covenant head (federal representative) of those they represent. Adam: federal head of all mankind in the covenant of works; his guilt and corruption imputed to all his descendants (Romans 5:12, 18-19). Christ: federal head of the elect in the covenant of grace; the last Adam (1 Corinthians 15:45) and second man (15:47) whose obedience and atoning death are imputed to all He represents (Romans 5:18-19). Grounded in the Adam-Christ parallel (Romans 5:12-21; 1 Corinthians 15:22). The structural backbone of Reformed covenant theology and soteriology: condemned in Adam, justified in Christ.

corruption_paragraphs: Federal headship is the substantive structure of the Reformed gospel, and the principal contests are with positions that deny one or both of its imputation-pillars. The Pelagian and semi-Pelagian denial of original sin denies the imputation of Adam's guilt to his posterity, treating each person as born morally neutral and responsible only for his own sins; this contradicts Romans 5:12-19's federal-headship structure. The New Perspective on Paul and various contemporary positions deny or reframe the imputation of Christ's active obedience, treating justification as covenant-membership status rather than the imputation of Christ's righteousness; this also contradicts the federal-headship structure (the parallel requires that just as Adam's disobedience is imputed to his race, Christ's obedience is imputed to His people). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive federal-headship doctrine: condemned in Adam our first federal head through the imputation of his sin; justified in Christ our second federal head through the imputation of His righteousness; the two imputations are the symmetrical pillars of the Reformed gospel.

etymology: The substantive comparison between two systems of biblical interpretation: dispensationalism (which divides redemptive history into distinct dispensations and maintains a sharp Israel-church distinction) and covenant theology (which reads redemptive history through the unified covenant of grace administered across successive periods). The principal interpretive divide within conservative Protestantism.
biblical_def: The substantive comparison between two systems of biblical interpretation that constitute the principal interpretive divide within conservative Protestantism. Dispensationalism (originating with John Nelson Darby and the Plymouth Brethren in the 1830s; popularized by the Scofield Reference Bible 1909, Dallas Theological Seminary, and the broader fundamentalist-evangelical world) divides redemptive history into distinct dispensations (typically seven: innocence, conscience, human government, promise, law, grace, kingdom) in which God deals with mankind under different administrative arrangements; it maintains a sharp and permanent distinction between Israel (God's earthly people with earthly promises) and the church (God's heavenly people, a parenthesis in the prophetic program); it typically holds to a pretribulational rapture, a literal future millennium centered on national Israel, and a futurist reading of prophecy. Covenant theology (the Reformed-confessional system; Westminster Confession VII; the broader Reformed tradition) reads redemptive history through the unified covenant of grace, administered through successive periods (Abrahamic, Mosaic, Davidic, New Covenant) but substantively one covenant with one people of God (the church, of which OT Israel was the typological form and the NT church the fulfillment); it reads the OT promises as fulfilled in Christ and the church; it typically holds to amillennial or postmillennial eschatology and a redemptive-historical reading of prophecy. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds covenant theology as the substantive Reformed-confessional system, rejecting dispensationalism's sharp Israel-church distinction (the church is not a parenthesis but the fulfillment of the covenant people; Galatians 3:29, if ye be Christ's, then are ye Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise; Ephesians 2:11-22, the one new man), its dispensational fragmentation of redemptive history, and its futurist-pretribulational eschatology.
webster_summary: Comparison between dispensationalism (distinct dispensations; sharp Israel-church distinction; pretribulational rapture; futurist prophecy) and covenant theology (unified covenant of grace; one people of God; redemptive-historical reading); the principal interpretive divide within conservative Protestantism.
webster_full: DISPENSATIONALISM vs. COVENANT THEOLOGY, n. phr. (theological systems comparison) The principal interpretive divide within conservative Protestantism. Dispensationalism (Darby, 1830s; Scofield Reference Bible 1909; Dallas Theological Seminary): divides redemptive history into distinct dispensations; maintains a sharp permanent Israel-church distinction (Israel earthly, church heavenly parenthesis); pretribulational rapture; literal future millennium centered on national Israel; futurist prophecy. Covenant theology (Reformed-confessional; Westminster VII): unified covenant of grace administered across successive periods; one people of God (church as fulfillment of OT Israel); OT promises fulfilled in Christ and the church; amillennial/postmillennial; redemptive-historical reading. Covenant theology rejects the sharp Israel-church distinction (Galatians 3:29; Ephesians 2:11-22).

corruption_paragraphs: The Reformed-confessional critique of dispensationalism focuses on its two principal errors. First, the sharp and permanent Israel-church distinction contradicts the NT teaching that the church is not a parenthesis in God's program but the fulfillment of the covenant people: believing Gentiles are grafted into the one olive tree (Romans 11:17-24); the believing Gentile is Abraham's seed and heir of the promise (Galatians 3:29); Christ has made Jew and Gentile one new man, breaking down the middle wall of partition (Ephesians 2:11-22). The church does not replace Israel (the supersessionist caricature) nor run on a separate track from Israel (the dispensational error); rather, the NT church is the eschatological fulfillment of the one covenant people, into which believing Jews and Gentiles are gathered. Second, the dispensational fragmentation of redemptive history into distinct administrative arrangements obscures the substantive unity of the covenant of grace across the testaments. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds covenant theology as the substantive Reformed-confessional system: one covenant of grace, administered across successive periods, with one people of God gathered from every nation into the body of Christ.

etymology: The Reformed-confessional doctrine that the one covenant of grace was administered differently under the Old Testament (by promises, prophecies, sacrifices, circumcision, the paschal lamb, and other types and ordinances) and under the New Testament (by the preaching of the Word and the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's Supper). Westminster Confession VII.5-6.
biblical_def: The Reformed-confessional doctrine that the one covenant of grace, substantively the same in every age, was administered differently under the Old Testament and the New Testament. Westminster Confession VII.5-6 articulates the doctrine: under the law (the OT), the covenant of grace was administered by promises, prophecies, sacrifices, circumcision, the paschal lamb, and other types and ordinances delivered to the people of the Jews, all foresignifying Christ to come; which were, for that time, sufficient and efficacious, through the operation of the Spirit, to instruct and build up the elect in faith in the promised Messiah (VII.5); under the gospel (the NT), when Christ, the substance, was exhibited, the ordinances in which this covenant is dispensed are the preaching of the Word, and the administration of the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's Supper: which, though fewer in number, and administered with more simplicity, and less outward glory, yet, in them, it is held forth in more fulness, evidence, and spiritual efficacy, to all nations, both Jews and Gentiles (VII.6). The substantive point is the unity of the covenant of grace across the two administrations: there are not therefore two covenants of grace, differing in substance, but one and the same, under various dispensations (VII.6). The OT and NT are not two different covenants of grace but two administrations of the one covenant of grace, the OT looking forward to Christ through types and shadows, the NT proclaiming the accomplished Christ through Word and sacrament. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine against both the dispensational fragmentation (which makes the OT and NT substantively different arrangements) and the flat-equation error (which ignores the genuine progression from type to fulfillment).
webster_summary: Reformed-confessional doctrine that the one covenant of grace was administered differently under the OT (promises, sacrifices, circumcision, types) and the NT (Word and sacraments); Westminster VII.5-6; not two covenants but one under various dispensations.
webster_full: ADMINISTRATIONS OF THE COVENANT, n. phr. (covenant theology) The one covenant of grace administered differently under the OT and NT. OT looks forward through types; NT proclaims accomplished Christ. Held against dispensational fragmentation and flat-equation error.

corruption_summary: The doctrine of the administrations of the covenant is held against dispensational fragmentation (two substantively different arrangements) and the flat-equation error (ignoring the progression from type to fulfillment).
corruption_paragraphs: The doctrine of the administrations of the covenant holds the substantive middle ground between two errors. The dispensational fragmentation makes the OT and NT substantively different arrangements (the OT a dispensation of law for earthly Israel, the NT a dispensation of grace for the heavenly church), obscuring the substantive unity of the covenant of grace across the testaments. The flat-equation error ignores the genuine progression from the OT administration (types, shadows, promises foresignifying Christ to come) to the NT administration (the accomplished Christ proclaimed through Word and sacrament). The Reformed-confessional doctrine holds both the unity (one covenant of grace, substantively the same) and the progression (administered by types and shadows under the OT, by Word and sacrament under the NT, with the NT holding the same covenant forth in more fulness, evidence, and spiritual efficacy). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine: the OT saints were saved by faith in the promised Messiah through the OT administration; the NT saints are saved by faith in the accomplished Christ through the NT administration; it is one covenant of grace, one people of God, administered in two ways across the progress of redemptive history.

etymology: The fundamental theological distinction between the law (which commands and condemns, revealing sin and driving the sinner to Christ) and the gospel (which freely offers salvation in Christ to the believing sinner). Central to both Lutheran and Reformed theology, though with substantive differences in emphasis and application.
biblical_def: The fundamental theological distinction between the law and the gospel. The law is God's commandment, which reveals His holy character, prescribes perfect obedience, exposes and condemns sin, and (for the unbeliever) drives him to despair of self-righteousness and (in the Spirit's work) to Christ. The gospel is the good news of salvation freely offered in Christ to the believing sinner — not a new law to be obeyed for salvation but the proclamation of what Christ has accomplished. The distinction is central to both Lutheran and Reformed theology, though with substantive differences. In Lutheran theology, the law-gospel distinction is the principal hermeneutical key: every text is to be rightly divided into law (which always accuses, lex semper accusat) and gospel (which always comforts); the law's principal use is to drive the sinner to Christ; the believer lives by the gospel. In Reformed theology, the law-gospel distinction is affirmed but held within the broader framework of the covenant of grace and the three uses of the law (especially the third use, the law as the rule of grateful obedience for the believer); the Reformed tradition emphasizes more strongly than Lutheran theology the abiding positive role of the law in the believer's sanctification. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive law-gospel distinction (the law commands and condemns; the gospel freely saves; justification is by the gospel through faith, not by the law through works) while holding it within the Reformed framework of the covenant of grace and the three uses of the law, affirming the abiding positive role of the moral law as the rule of the believer's grateful obedience (against the antinomian misuse of the law-gospel distinction to dismiss the law's third use).
webster_summary: The fundamental distinction between the law (which commands and condemns, driving the sinner to Christ) and the gospel (which freely offers salvation in Christ); central to Lutheran and Reformed theology, with the Reformed tradition emphasizing the law's abiding third use in sanctification.
webster_full: LAW AND GOSPEL, n. phr. (Reformed and Lutheran theology) The distinction between the law (God's commandment, which reveals His character, prescribes perfect obedience, exposes and condemns sin, drives the sinner to Christ) and the gospel (the good news of salvation freely offered in Christ to the believing sinner). Central to both Lutheran and Reformed theology. Lutheran: the principal hermeneutical key; law always accuses (lex semper accusat), gospel always comforts. Reformed: affirmed but held within the covenant of grace and the three uses of the law, emphasizing the law's abiding third use (the rule of grateful obedience). Held against the antinomian misuse that dismisses the law's third use.

corruption_paragraphs: The law-gospel distinction is held against two opposing misuses. The legalist misuse confuses law and gospel, making justification depend on the sinner's law-keeping; this contradicts the gospel's free offer of salvation in Christ apart from works (Romans 3:20, 28; Galatians 2:16). The antinomian misuse abuses the law-gospel distinction to dismiss the law's abiding positive role in the believer's life; treating the law as wholly negative (only accusing, never guiding), the antinomian denies the third use of the law (the moral law as the rule of the believer's grateful obedience). The Reformed-confessional tradition holds the substantive law-gospel distinction (justification is by the gospel through faith, not by the law through works) while affirming the abiding positive role of the moral law (the third use, the rule of grateful obedience in sanctification). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the Reformed framework: the law commands and condemns the unbeliever, driving him to Christ; the gospel freely saves the believing sinner; the moral law continues as the rule of the justified believer's grateful obedience, written on the heart by the Spirit in the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:33; Hebrews 8:10).

etymology: The Reformed-confessional doctrine that the moral law of God serves three uses: (1) the civil use (restraining sin in society); (2) the pedagogical use (revealing sin and driving the sinner to Christ); (3) the normative use (the rule of grateful obedience for the believer). Articulated by Calvin (Institutes II.7) and the Reformed confessions; the Reformed tradition especially emphasizes the third use.
biblical_def: The Reformed-confessional doctrine that the moral law of God serves three distinct uses in the divine economy. (1) The civil or political use (usus politicus or usus civilis): the law restrains sin and evil in society by the threat of punishment, preserving civil order and curbing the wickedness of even the unregenerate (1 Timothy 1:9-10, the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient). (2) The pedagogical or convicting use (usus paedagogicus or usus elenchticus): the law reveals sin, exposes the sinner's guilt, strips away self-righteousness, and (in the Spirit's work) drives the sinner to despair of self and to flee to Christ (Romans 3:20, by the law is the knowledge of sin; Galatians 3:24, the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ). (3) The normative or didactic use (usus normativus or tertius usus legis, the third use): the law serves as the rule of grateful obedience for the justified believer, guiding him in the path of holiness and revealing the will of God for the Christian life (Psalm 119, the believer's delight in the law; Romans 7:22, I delight in the law of God after the inward man; the moral law written on the heart in the new covenant, Jeremiah 31:33). Calvin articulated the three uses in the Institutes (II.7); the Reformed tradition (unlike some Lutheran formulations that emphasize the second use as the principal use) especially emphasizes the third use as the abiding positive role of the law in the believer's sanctification. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive three-uses doctrine, especially the third use against the antinomian denial of the law's abiding positive role.
webster_summary: Reformed doctrine that the moral law serves three uses: (1) civil (restraining sin in society); (2) pedagogical (revealing sin, driving to Christ); (3) normative/third use (the rule of grateful obedience for the believer); Calvin Institutes II.7; the Reformed tradition emphasizes the third use.
webster_full: THREE USES OF THE LAW, n. phr. (Reformed theology) The moral law serves three uses. (1) Civil/political use (usus civilis): restrains sin in society by threat of punishment, preserving civil order (1 Timothy 1:9-10). (2) Pedagogical/convicting use (usus paedagogicus): reveals sin, exposes guilt, drives the sinner to Christ (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:24). (3) Normative/didactic use (tertius usus legis, the third use): the rule of grateful obedience for the justified believer, guiding him in holiness (Psalm 119; Romans 7:22; the law written on the heart, Jeremiah 31:33). Calvin Institutes II.7. The Reformed tradition especially emphasizes the third use as the law's abiding positive role; held against the antinomian denial.

corruption_paragraphs: The principal contemporary contest over the three uses of the law concerns the third use. The antinomian position (in its various forms, from the historic antinomian controversies to contemporary hyper-grace and easy-believism) denies the third use of the law, treating the law as wholly negative (only restraining the wicked and convicting the sinner, never guiding the believer); the antinomian holds that the believer who is free from the law's condemnation is also free from the law's direction. The Reformed-confessional tradition rejects this: the moral law continues as the rule of the justified believer's grateful obedience (the third use), written on the heart by the Spirit in the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:33; Hebrews 8:10), delighted in by the regenerate believer (Psalm 119; Romans 7:22). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive three-uses doctrine with particular emphasis on the third use: the believer is freed from the law's condemnation (the law cannot condemn the one who is in Christ, Romans 8:1) but not from the law's direction (the moral law remains the rule of his grateful obedience); the Christian life is the Spirit-empowered obedience to the moral law out of grateful love for the God who saved him, not the antinomian disregard of the law's abiding direction.

etymology: The Reformed-confessional threefold division of the Mosaic law into moral law (the Ten Commandments, perpetually binding), ceremonial law (the ritual-sacrificial-typological law, abrogated in Christ), and judicial law (the civil law of national Israel, expired except for its general equity). Westminster Confession XIX.
biblical_def: The Reformed-confessional threefold division of the Mosaic law, articulated in Westminster Confession XIX. (1) The moral law: summarized in the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20; Deuteronomy 5), it expresses God's perpetual moral will, binds all people in all ages, and continues as the rule of righteousness for both the unbeliever (whom it condemns) and the believer (whom it guides, the third use). The moral law is grounded in God's unchanging holy character and was written on the heart at creation (Romans 2:14-15); it is not abrogated but fulfilled and established by Christ (Matthew 5:17-19; Romans 3:31). (2) The ceremonial law: the ritual, sacrificial, dietary, purity, and festival laws that typologically foresignified Christ and His work; these were a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ (Colossians 2:17; Hebrews 10:1), and are abrogated in Christ, who fulfilled and thereby ended them (Hebrews 8-10; the dietary laws set aside, Mark 7:19; Acts 10). (3) The judicial (civil) law: the civil-legal code given to Israel as a national-theocratic body (laws of property, courts, punishments, civil order); these expired together with the State of that people, not obliging any other now, further than the general equity thereof may require (Westminster XIX.4). The substantive principle of general equity: while the specific Israelite-theocratic applications have expired, the underlying just principles (general equity) continue to inform the civil order. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive threefold division: the moral law is perpetually binding; the ceremonial law is abrogated in Christ; the judicial law has expired except for its general equity. The threefold division is essential for rightly handling the Mosaic law in the Christian life, distinguishing what continues (the moral law, the general equity of the judicial law) from what is abrogated (the ceremonial law, the specific Israelite-theocratic judicial applications).
webster_summary: Reformed-confessional threefold division of the Mosaic law: moral (Ten Commandments, perpetually binding), ceremonial (ritual-typological, abrogated in Christ), judicial (civil law of national Israel, expired except for general equity); Westminster XIX.
webster_full: MORAL, CEREMONIAL, JUDICIAL LAW, n. phr. (Reformed theology) The threefold division of the Mosaic law (Westminster XIX). (1) Moral law: the Ten Commandments; expresses God's perpetual moral will; binds all people in all ages; grounded in God's unchanging character (Romans 2:14-15); fulfilled and established (not abrogated) by Christ (Matthew 5:17-19). (2) Ceremonial law: ritual, sacrificial, dietary, purity, festival laws typologically foresignifying Christ; a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ (Colossians 2:17); abrogated in Christ (Hebrews 8-10; Mark 7:19; Acts 10). (3) Judicial/civil law: the civil code of national-theocratic Israel; expired together with the State of that people... further than the general equity thereof may require (Westminster XIX.4).

corruption_summary: The threefold division is essential for rightly handling the Mosaic law; errors arise from collapsing the categories (treating all Mosaic law as either wholly binding or wholly abrogated) rather than distinguishing the perpetual moral law from the abrogated ceremonial and expired judicial.
corruption_paragraphs: The threefold division of the Mosaic law is essential for rightly handling the law in the Christian life, and errors arise from collapsing the categories. The antinomian error treats all the Mosaic law (including the moral law) as abrogated in Christ, leaving the believer with no abiding moral standard; this contradicts Christ's affirmation that He came not to destroy but to fulfill the law (Matthew 5:17-19) and the NT's continuing affirmation of the moral law (Romans 13:8-10; the apostolic citations of the Ten Commandments). The legalistic and the Judaizing error treats all the Mosaic law (including the ceremonial law) as perpetually binding, requiring Christians to keep the dietary laws, the festivals, circumcision, etc.; this contradicts the NT's clear teaching that the ceremonial law is abrogated in Christ (Colossians 2:16-17; Hebrews 8-10; the Jerusalem Council, Acts 15). The Reformed-confessional threefold division holds the substantive distinctions: the moral law (the Ten Commandments) is perpetually binding; the ceremonial law is abrogated in Christ who fulfilled it; the judicial law has expired with national Israel except for its general equity. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive division as the key to rightly handling the Mosaic law — honoring the perpetual moral law, recognizing the fulfilled-and-abrogated ceremonial law, and applying the general equity of the judicial law to the civil order.

etymology: From Greek typos (type, pattern, figure). The biblical-interpretive discipline that identifies persons, events, institutions, and objects in the Old Testament (types) as divinely-designed foreshadowings of corresponding realities in the New Testament (antitypes), supremely Christ and His work. Grounded in the NT's own typological reading of the OT.
biblical_def: From Greek typos (type, pattern, figure, impression); the biblical-interpretive discipline that identifies persons, events, institutions, and objects in the Old Testament (types) as divinely-designed foreshadowings of corresponding realities in the New Testament (antitypes), supremely the person and work of Christ. Biblical typology is not arbitrary allegory imposed on the text but the recognition of divinely-intended patterns that the NT itself identifies. The NT explicitly reads the OT typologically: Adam is a type (Greek typos) of Christ (Romans 5:14); the wilderness events are types (1 Corinthians 10:6, 11, these things were our examples [typoi]... they are written for our admonition); the Passover lamb foreshadows Christ our Passover (1 Corinthians 5:7; John 1:29); the tabernacle and its furnishings are a shadow of heavenly realities (Hebrews 8-10); the Melchizedek priesthood foreshadows Christ's priesthood (Hebrews 7); Jonah's three days foreshadow Christ's burial and resurrection (Matthew 12:40); the brazen serpent foreshadows Christ lifted up (John 3:14-15); the flood and the Red Sea foreshadow baptism (1 Peter 3:21; 1 Corinthians 10:2); Isaac, Joseph, David, Solomon, and many others foreshadow Christ in various respects. The substantive interpretive principles: typology is grounded in the divinely-intended unity of redemptive history; the type genuinely foreshadows the antitype by God's design; the antitype is greater than the type (Christ is greater than Adam, Moses, David, Solomon, Jonah, the temple, etc.); typology is controlled by the NT's own typological readings and by the analogy of Scripture, not by arbitrary allegorical fancy. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds substantive biblical typology as a key discipline of redemptive-historical interpretation, distinguishing it from both the wooden literalism that misses the typological dimension and the arbitrary allegorism that imposes meanings the text does not bear.

corruption_paragraphs: Biblical typology is held between two interpretive errors. The wooden-literalist error misses the typological dimension of the OT entirely, reading the OT persons, events, and institutions as mere historical data without recognizing the divinely-intended foreshadowings of Christ that the NT identifies; this impoverishes the reading of the OT and severs it from its fulfillment in Christ. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds substantive biblical typology under proper controls: typology is grounded in the divinely-intended unity of redemptive history; the type genuinely foreshadows the antitype by God's design (not by the interpreter's fancy); the antitype is greater than the type; typology is controlled by the NT's own typological readings (Adam, the Passover, the tabernacle, Melchizedek, the brazen serpent, etc.) and by the analogy of Scripture. Substantive typology is a key discipline of redemptive-historical interpretation, opening the OT as the divinely-designed shadow of the Christ who fulfills it.

etymology: The biblical-theological pattern by which the Old Testament promises (the protoevangelium, the Abrahamic promises, the Davidic promises, the prophetic promises of the new covenant and the Messiah) are fulfilled in the New Testament in the person and work of Christ. The structural relationship between the testaments in covenant theology and Reformed biblical theology.
biblical_def: The biblical-theological pattern by which the Old Testament promises are fulfilled in the New Testament in the person and work of Christ. The pattern is the structural relationship between the testaments in covenant theology and Reformed biblical theology, expressing the substantive unity of redemptive history while honoring its genuine progression. The OT is the era of promise: the protoevangelium (the first gospel-promise, Genesis 3:15, the seed of the woman who will crush the serpent's head); the Abrahamic promises (the seed, the land, the blessing to all nations, Genesis 12:1-3; 15; 17); the Davidic promises (the everlasting throne, the son who will reign forever, 2 Samuel 7); the prophetic promises (the new covenant, Jeremiah 31:31-34; the suffering servant, Isaiah 53; the coming Messiah, the outpoured Spirit, the gathered nations). The NT is the era of fulfillment: all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen (2 Corinthians 1:20); Christ is the fulfillment of the law and the prophets (Matthew 5:17); the gospel is the promise made to the fathers now fulfilled (Acts 13:32-33); Christ is the seed of the woman, the seed of Abraham (Galatians 3:16), the son of David (Matthew 1:1), the suffering servant, the mediator of the new covenant (Hebrews 8-9). The substantive interpretive principle: the OT promises are not abandoned, spiritualized away, or fulfilled in a different program (the dispensational error) but are genuinely fulfilled in Christ and His church, often in ways that exceed and transform the original form of the promise (the land promise fulfilled in the new creation; the throne promise fulfilled in Christ's heavenly reign; the seed promise fulfilled in Christ and those in Him). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive promise-and-fulfillment pattern as the key to reading the two testaments together: the OT promises, the NT fulfills; the whole of Scripture is the unfolding of the one redemptive plan climaxing in Christ.

The NT is the era of fulfillment: all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen (2 Corinthians 1:20); Christ fulfills the law and prophets (Matthew 5:17); the seed of Abraham (Galatians 3:16), son of David (Matthew 1:1), mediator of the new covenant. The promises are genuinely fulfilled in Christ and His church, not abandoned or fulfilled in a separate program.

etymology: From Genesis 3:15, the protoevangelium (first gospel-promise), where God promises that the seed of the woman will crush the serpent's head while the serpent bruises his heel. The foundational messianic promise that runs through the whole of Scripture, fulfilled in Christ, the seed of the woman who crushes Satan.
biblical_def: From Genesis 3:15, the protoevangelium (first gospel-promise), the foundational messianic promise that runs through the whole of Scripture. In the immediate aftermath of the Fall, God pronounces judgment on the serpent and embeds within the curse the first promise of redemption: And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel (Genesis 3:15). The promise establishes the substantive structure of redemptive history: there will be enmity between the serpent's seed (the children of the devil, those in rebellion against God) and the woman's seed (the line of promise, culminating in the one great Seed); the woman's seed will crush the serpent's head (a mortal wound, decisive victory) while the serpent will bruise the seed's heel (a real but non-fatal wound, the suffering of Christ). The promise is fulfilled in Christ: He is the seed of the woman (born of a woman, Galatians 4:4); He crushes the serpent's head at the cross and resurrection (Hebrews 2:14, that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil; Colossians 2:15, the principalities and powers spoiled and triumphed over; 1 John 3:8, the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the devil); the serpent bruises His heel in the suffering of the cross. The promise is extended to the church: the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly (Romans 16:20), the church sharing in Christ's victory over the serpent. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the seed-of-the-woman promise as the foundational thread of biblical theology: from Genesis 3:15 through the line of promise (Seth, Noah, Abraham, Judah, David) to Christ the great Seed, the whole of Scripture is the unfolding of the protoevangelium, the war between the two seeds, climaxing in Christ's decisive crushing of the serpent.
webster_summary: From Genesis 3:15, the protoevangelium: God's promise that the seed of the woman will crush the serpent's head while the serpent bruises his heel; the foundational messianic promise fulfilled in Christ, who crushes Satan at the cross and resurrection (Hebrews 2:14; Colossians 2:15; 1 John 3:8).
webster_full: SEED OF THE WOMAN, n. phr. Fulfilled in Christ: the seed of the woman (Galatians 4:4); crushes the serpent at the cross and resurrection (Hebrews 2:14; Colossians 2:15; 1 John 3:8). Extended to the church (Romans 16:20). The foundational thread of biblical theology from Genesis 3:15 to Christ.

etymology: The covenant-theological principle do this and live (Leviticus 18:5; Romans 10:5; Galatians 3:12) by which the covenant of works operated: perfect obedience as the condition of life. Distinguished from the grace principle (the free gift of life through faith in Christ) that governs the covenant of grace.
biblical_def: The covenant-theological principle do this and live by which the covenant of works operated: perfect, personal, perpetual obedience as the condition of life and blessing. The principle is summarized in Leviticus 18:5 (Ye shall therefore keep my statutes, and my judgments: which if a man do, he shall live in them), cited by Paul as the principle of law-righteousness (Romans 10:5, Moses describeth the righteousness which is of the law, That the man which doeth those things shall live by them; Galatians 3:12, the law is not of faith: but, The man that doeth them shall live in them). The works principle governed the covenant of works with Adam: perfect obedience was the condition of confirmed life; Adam's disobedience brought death (Genesis 2:17). After the Fall, no fallen sinner can meet the works principle (Romans 3:20, by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified; Galatians 2:16); the works principle now functions to expose the impossibility of self-righteousness and to drive the sinner to Christ. Crucially, the works principle is met by Christ as the second Adam: Christ alone rendered the perfect obedience that the works principle requires (His active obedience), and His obedience is imputed to His people. The substantive contrast is between the works principle (do this and live, the principle of the covenant of works, met only by Christ) and the grace principle (the free gift of life through faith in Christ, the principle of the covenant of grace). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive distinction: the works principle reveals the impossible standard of perfect obedience that condemns the sinner; Christ alone met the works principle by His perfect active obedience; the sinner is justified not by his own works (which can never meet the works principle) but by Christ's works imputed to him through faith (the grace principle).
webster_summary: The covenant-theological principle do this and live (Leviticus 18:5; Romans 10:5; Galatians 3:12): perfect obedience as the condition of life; governed the covenant of works; unmeetable by fallen sinners; met only by Christ the second Adam; distinguished from the grace principle.
webster_full: WORKS PRINCIPLE, n. phr. (covenant theology) The principle do this and live: perfect, personal, perpetual obedience as the condition of life and blessing. Met only by Christ the second Adam (His active obedience imputed to His people). Distinguished from the grace principle (free gift of life through faith).

corruption_paragraphs: The works principle is the standard of perfect obedience that the covenant of works required and that no fallen sinner can meet. The legalist error treats the works principle as the way of salvation, supposing that the sinner can do this and live by his own obedience; this contradicts the NT's clear teaching that by the deeds of the law no flesh shall be justified (Romans 3:20; Galatians 2:16). The substantive gospel is that Christ kept the covenant of works for us, that we might receive the covenant of grace freely.

etymology: The covenant-theological principle by which the covenant of grace operates: salvation as the free gift of God received through faith in Christ, not earned by works. Contrasted with the works principle (do this and live). Romans 4:4-5; 11:6; Ephesians 2:8-9.
biblical_def: The covenant-theological principle by which the covenant of grace operates: salvation as the free gift of God, received through faith in Christ, not earned by the sinner's works. The principle is contrasted throughout Scripture with the works principle (do this and live). Paul articulates the contrast sharply: Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt. But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness (Romans 4:4-5); And if by grace, then is it no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace. But if it be of works, then is it no more grace: otherwise work is no more work (Romans 11:6); For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast (Ephesians 2:8-9). The grace principle and the works principle are mutually exclusive as ways of salvation: salvation is either earned by works (the works principle, which the sinner cannot meet) or received as a free gift through faith (the grace principle). The substantive structure of Reformed soteriology rests on the grace principle: the sinner cannot meet the works principle (perfect obedience); Christ met the works principle on his behalf (active obedience) and bore the penalty of the broken works principle (passive obedience, the atoning death); the sinner receives the benefits of Christ's work freely through faith (the grace principle); justification is by grace alone (sola gratia) through faith alone (sola fide) in Christ alone (solus Christus). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive grace principle as the heart of the gospel: salvation is the free gift of God, received through faith in Christ, grounded in Christ's meeting of the works principle on the sinner's behalf, excluding all boasting in the sinner's own works.
webster_summary: The covenant-theological principle by which the covenant of grace operates: salvation as the free gift of God received through faith in Christ, not earned by works; contrasted with the works principle; Romans 4:4-5; 11:6; Ephesians 2:8-9; the heart of Reformed soteriology (sola gratia).
webster_full: GRACE PRINCIPLE, n. phr. (covenant theology) Salvation as the free gift of God, received through faith in Christ, not earned by works. Contrasted with the works principle (do this and live). Paul's sharp articulation: to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness (Romans 4:4-5); if by grace, then is it no more of works (Romans 11:6); by grace are ye saved through faith... not of works, lest any man should boast (Ephesians 2:8-9). The grace and works principles are mutually exclusive as ways of salvation. The heart of Reformed soteriology: the sinner cannot meet the works principle; Christ met it on his behalf; the sinner receives the benefits freely through faith. Sola gratia, sola fide, solus Christus.

corruption_paragraphs: The grace principle is held against two opposing errors. The legalist error mixes works into the grace principle, making salvation depend partly on the sinner's works; this contradicts Paul's sharp insistence that grace and works are mutually exclusive as ways of salvation (Romans 11:6, if by grace, then is it no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace). The Roman Catholic system of infused grace and meritorious works, the Galatian Judaizing error, and every form of works-righteousness violate the grace principle. The antinomian error abuses the grace principle to dismiss the law's abiding positive role (the third use), supposing that because salvation is by grace apart from works, the believer is free from the law's direction; this confuses the ground of justification (grace alone, apart from works) with the rule of sanctification (the moral law as the rule of grateful obedience). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive grace principle as the heart of the gospel: salvation is the free gift of God, received through faith in Christ, grounded in Christ's meeting of the works principle on the sinner's behalf (His active obedience imputed, His penalty borne), excluding all boasting in the sinner's own works (Ephesians 2:8-9) — while affirming that the grace that saves also sanctifies, producing the good works that are the fruit (not the ground) of salvation (Ephesians 2:10).

etymology: The medieval-scholastic and Roman Catholic distinction between condign merit (meritum de condigno, merit strictly deserving of reward by justice) and congruent merit (meritum de congruo, merit fittingly rewarded by God's gracious arrangement). The Reformed-confessional tradition rejects all human merit in justification, holding that only Christ's merit avails.
biblical_def: The medieval-scholastic and Roman Catholic theological distinction between two kinds of merit. Condign merit (meritum de condigno): merit that is strictly deserving of reward by justice, such that God would be unjust not to reward it; in the Catholic system, the works of the justified person (performed in a state of grace) are held to be condignly meritorious of an increase of grace and of eternal life. Congruent merit (meritum de congruo): merit that is not strictly deserving but is fittingly rewarded by God's gracious arrangement; in the Catholic system, the works of the person not yet in a state of grace (or certain preparatory works) are held to be congruently meritorious of the grace of justification. The Reformed-confessional tradition rejects all human merit in justification. The grounds for rejection: (1) fallen human works cannot merit before God, since even the believer's best works are imperfect and tainted by sin (Isaiah 64:6, all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags); (2) salvation is by grace, not merit (Romans 4:4-5; 11:6; Ephesians 2:8-9); (3) only Christ's merit avails — the believer is justified by the imputed merit of Christ (His active and passive obedience), not by any merit of his own. The Reformed tradition does affirm that God graciously rewards the believer's works (the believer's good works, performed by the Spirit's grace, are rewarded by God's gracious promise, not by strict desert), but this is a reward of grace, not of merit. The patriarchal-Reformed reader rejects the condign-congruent merit scheme: no human work, before or after justification, merits anything from God; the believer is justified by Christ's merit alone, imputed through faith; the believer's good works are the fruit of grace and are graciously (not meritoriously) rewarded.

etymology: From Latin imputare (to reckon, charge to one's account); Greek logizomai (to reckon, count, impute). The Reformed-confessional doctrine that God credits or reckons something to a person's account that is not inherently theirs: Adam's sin imputed to his posterity, the believer's sin imputed to Christ, and Christ's righteousness imputed to the believer. The threefold imputation that structures Reformed soteriology.
biblical_def: From Latin imputare (to reckon, charge to one's account); the Reformed-confessional doctrine that God credits or reckons something to a person's account that is not inherently their own. The Greek logizomai (to reckon, count, impute) is the key NT term, used eleven times in Romans 4 alone. The doctrine involves a threefold imputation that structures the whole of Reformed soteriology. (1) The imputation of Adam's sin to his posterity: Adam's first sin is reckoned to the account of all his natural descendants, so that all are born guilty and corrupt in him (Romans 5:12-19; the doctrine of original sin). (2) The imputation of the believer's sin to Christ: the sins of God's people are reckoned to Christ's account, so that He bore their guilt and its penalty on the cross (Isaiah 53:6, the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all; 2 Corinthians 5:21, he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; 1 Peter 2:24, who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree). (3) The imputation of Christ's righteousness to the believer: the perfect righteousness of Christ (His active obedience to the law and His passive obedience in bearing its penalty) is reckoned to the account of the believing sinner, so that he is justified — declared righteous — not on the basis of his own righteousness but on the basis of Christ's righteousness imputed to him (Romans 4:3-8, Abraham's faith counted for righteousness; 2 Corinthians 5:21, that we might be made the righteousness of God in him; Philippians 3:9, the righteousness which is of God by faith). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive threefold imputation as the structural backbone of Reformed soteriology: condemned through Adam's imputed sin; redeemed through our sin imputed to Christ; justified through Christ's righteousness imputed to us. The doctrine of imputation (especially the imputation of Christ's righteousness) is the heart of the Reformation doctrine of justification, denied by Rome (which holds justification to be by infused, not imputed, righteousness) and by the New Perspective on Paul (which reframes justification as covenant-membership status).

(3) Christ's righteousness imputed to the believer (Romans 4:3-8; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9, the righteousness which is of God by faith). corruption_paragraphs: The doctrine of imputation, especially the imputation of Christ's righteousness, is the heart of the Reformation doctrine of justification, and it is denied by two principal positions. The Roman Catholic position holds that justification is by infused righteousness, not imputed righteousness: God does not merely reckon Christ's righteousness to the believer's account (declaring him righteous) but infuses righteousness into the believer (making him actually righteous), so that justification is a process of becoming righteous rather than a declaration of righteous standing; this confuses justification with sanctification and grounds the believer's standing partly in his own infused-and-cooperated-with righteousness. The New Perspective on Paul reframes justification as covenant-membership status (the declaration that one is a member of the covenant people) rather than the imputation of Christ's righteousness, denying or marginalizing the imputation of Christ's active obedience. The Reformed-confessional tradition holds the substantive imputation doctrine: justification is the forensic declaration that the believing sinner is righteous, on the basis of Christ's righteousness imputed (reckoned) to his account through faith; the believer's standing rests entirely on Christ's imputed righteousness, not on any righteousness of his own (infused or otherwise). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive threefold imputation as the structural backbone of the gospel: condemned in Adam, redeemed through our sin laid on Christ, justified through Christ's righteousness reckoned to us — the great exchange (2 Corinthians 5:21) at the heart of the gospel.

etymology: The intra-Reformed debate over whether the covenant of works was in some sense republished in the Mosaic covenant at Sinai. The republication position holds that the Mosaic covenant included a republication of the works principle (in some formulation); the anti-republication position holds that the Mosaic covenant was an administration of the covenant of grace without a works-principle republication.
biblical_def: The intra-Reformed debate over whether, and in what sense, the covenant of works was republished in the Mosaic covenant at Sinai. The debate concerns the precise relationship between the Mosaic covenant and the covenant of works / covenant of grace. The republication position (held by some in the older Reformed tradition and revived in contemporary discussion, notably by some at Westminster Seminary California) holds that the Mosaic covenant, while an administration of the covenant of grace at the level of eternal salvation, included in some sense a republication of the works principle (do this and live, Leviticus 18:5) — whether with respect to Israel's tenure in the land (a national, typological works-principle governing Israel's temporal blessing and curse in Canaan) or in some other formulation. The republication position appeals to the Pauline contrast between the law and the promise (Galatians 3; Romans 10:5 citing Leviticus 18:5 as the law-principle), the Sinai covenant's conditional blessing-and-curse structure (Deuteronomy 27-28), and the older Reformed sources that spoke of the law as a republication of the covenant of works in some sense. The anti-republication position (held by other contemporary Reformed theologians) holds that the Mosaic covenant was wholly an administration of the covenant of grace, with the law functioning pedagogically (driving to Christ) and normatively (the rule of grateful obedience) but without a works-principle republication; this position emphasizes the gracious character of the Sinai covenant (the LORD redeemed Israel from Egypt before giving the law, Exodus 20:2) and warns that the republication position risks compromising the unity of the covenant of grace. The patriarchal-Reformed reader engages the republication debate as a substantive intra-Reformed discussion; both positions are held within the confessional Reformed tradition with substantive theological integrity, and the debate concerns the precise formulation of the Mosaic covenant's relationship to the works and grace principles, not a gospel-essential disagreement.

Appeals to Galatians 3; Romans 10:5; Deuteronomy 27-28. Anti-republication position: the Mosaic covenant was wholly an administration of the covenant of grace; the law functions pedagogically and normatively without a works-principle republication; emphasizes the gracious character of Sinai (Exodus 20:2).

etymology: The covenant-theological question of what continues and what changes between the Old and New Testaments. Covenant theology emphasizes continuity (one covenant of grace, one people of God); dispensationalism emphasizes discontinuity (distinct dispensations, Israel-church distinction); the precise balance is debated across the spectrum of Reformed and broadly evangelical positions.
biblical_def: The covenant-theological question of what continues and what changes between the Old and New Testaments — the proper balance between continuity (what remains the same) and discontinuity (what changes) across the testaments. The question structures much of the debate between and within the major interpretive systems. Covenant theology emphasizes continuity: one covenant of grace administered across the testaments; one people of God (the church, of which OT Israel was the typological form); the moral law continuing; the covenant signs continuing (circumcision-baptism); the substantive unity of the people of God and the plan of salvation. Dispensationalism emphasizes discontinuity: distinct dispensations with different administrative arrangements; a sharp Israel-church distinction; the law-grace contrast as marking different programs. Between these poles, various positions occupy the spectrum: New Covenant Theology (a position emphasizing more discontinuity than covenant theology but less than dispensationalism, holding that the Mosaic law as a unit is abrogated and replaced by the law of Christ); progressive covenantalism (a recent mediating position); and various nuanced Reformed positions on the precise continuity and discontinuity of the law, the covenant signs, the people of God, and the kingdom. The substantive questions include: the continuity/discontinuity of the moral law (the threefold division); the continuity/discontinuity of the covenant signs (circumcision-baptism, the paedobaptist-credobaptist debate); the continuity/discontinuity of the people of God (Israel-church); the continuity/discontinuity of the Sabbath; the continuity/discontinuity of the land promise. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the covenant-theological emphasis on continuity (one covenant of grace, one people of God, the continuing moral law, the substantive unity of redemptive history) while honoring the genuine discontinuities (the abrogation of the ceremonial law, the change of covenant signs, the progression from type to fulfillment, the greater fulness of the new covenant administration).

etymology: The Reformed-confessional doctrine that the ceremonial law of Moses (the ritual, sacrificial, dietary, purity, and festival laws) was abrogated in Christ, who fulfilled the types and shadows it foresignified. Westminster Confession XIX.3; Colossians 2:16-17; Hebrews 8-10.
biblical_def: The Reformed-confessional doctrine that the ceremonial law of Moses was abrogated in Christ, who fulfilled the types and shadows it foresignified. The ceremonial law comprises the ritual, sacrificial, dietary, purity, festival, and tabernacle/temple laws given to Israel (Westminster XIX.3 calls them ceremonial laws, containing several typical ordinances, partly of worship, prefiguring Christ, his graces, actions, sufferings, and benefits; and partly, holding forth divers instructions of moral duties). These laws were a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ (Colossians 2:17). With the coming of Christ, the substance to which the shadows pointed, the ceremonial law was fulfilled and thereby abrogated. The substantive NT teaching: (1) the sacrificial system is fulfilled and abrogated in Christ's once-for-all sacrifice (Hebrews 8-10; by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified, Hebrews 10:14; the temple sacrifices rendered obsolete); (2) the dietary laws are set aside (Mark 7:19, purging all meats; Acts 10:9-16, Peter's vision; 1 Timothy 4:3-5, every creature of God good and to be received with thanksgiving); (3) the festival and Sabbath-ceremonial observances are fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16-17; the Passover fulfilled in Christ our Passover, 1 Corinthians 5:7); (4) circumcision is replaced by baptism (Colossians 2:11-12); (5) the temple is fulfilled in Christ and His body (John 2:19-21; 1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21). Westminster XIX.3: All which ceremonial laws are now abrogated, under the new testament. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine: the ceremonial law is abrogated in Christ; the Christian is not bound to keep the dietary laws, the festivals, the sacrifices, circumcision, or the other ceremonial observances; these have been fulfilled by Christ the substance to which they pointed. The doctrine is held against both the Judaizing error (which would re-impose the ceremonial law on Christians) and the antinomian error (which would extend the abrogation to the moral law).

corruption_paragraphs: The doctrine of the abrogated ceremonial law is held against two opposing errors. The Judaizing error would re-impose the ceremonial law on Christians, requiring them to keep the dietary laws, observe the festivals, undergo circumcision, etc.; this was the error of the Galatian Judaizers that Paul vigorously opposed (Galatians; the Jerusalem Council, Acts 15) and recurs in various forms (Hebrew Roots movement, certain Sabbatarian-festival movements). The NT teaching is clear: the ceremonial law is fulfilled in Christ the substance; to re-impose the shadow after the substance has come is to deny the sufficiency of Christ's fulfillment (Colossians 2:16-17; Galatians 4:9-11; 5:2-4). The antinomian error would extend the abrogation of the ceremonial law to the moral law, supposing that because the ceremonial law is abrogated, the moral law (the Ten Commandments) is also abrogated; this confuses the categories of the threefold division. The Reformed-confessional doctrine holds the substantive distinction: the ceremonial law is abrogated in Christ; the moral law continues as perpetually binding. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine: the Christian is not bound to keep the dietary laws, the festivals, the sacrifices, circumcision, or the other ceremonial observances (these are fulfilled in Christ); but the moral law continues as the rule of grateful obedience. The ceremonial law is not abolished as worthless but fulfilled as having reached its substance in Christ; the believer reads the ceremonial law typologically, seeing Christ in the sacrifices, the priesthood, the tabernacle, the festivals, and the whole ceremonial system.

etymology: The Reformed-confessional doctrine (Westminster Confession XIX.4) that the judicial (civil) law given to national Israel expired with the Israelite state, except for its general equity — the underlying just principles that continue to inform the civil order. Distinguished from theonomy (which would apply the Mosaic judicial law more directly).
biblical_def: The Reformed-confessional doctrine (Westminster Confession XIX.4) governing the contemporary status of the judicial (civil) law of Moses. The judicial law comprises the civil-legal code given to Israel as a national-theocratic body: the laws of property, contracts, courts, punishments, civil administration, and national life. Westminster XIX.4 states: To them also, as a body politic, he gave sundry judicial laws, which expired together with the State of that people; not obliging any other now, further than the general equity thereof may require. The substantive doctrine has two parts. (1) The specific Israelite-theocratic judicial laws expired with national Israel: the particular civil applications given to Israel as a national-theocratic body (the specific penalties, the specific civil arrangements, the specific theocratic provisions) are not binding on other nations now, because they were given to Israel as a unique national-theocratic body that has passed away with the coming of Christ and the dissolution of the OT theocracy. (2) The general equity continues to oblige: the underlying just principles embedded in the judicial law (the general equity, the substantive justice the laws expressed) continue to inform the civil order and to instruct the Christian magistrate. For example, the specific Mosaic law requiring a parapet around a flat roof (Deuteronomy 22:8) is not binding as a specific civil statute, but its general equity (the principle that one must take reasonable measures to prevent harm to others on one's property) continues to oblige. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive general-equity doctrine, distinguishing it from two opposing positions. Theonomy (the Reconstructionist position of R. J. Rushdoony, Greg Bahnsen, and others) would apply the Mosaic judicial law (including its specific penalties) more directly and comprehensively to the modern civil order. webster_full: JUDICIAL LAW AND GENERAL EQUITY, n. phr. The judicial law remains a source of wisdom for the Christian magistrate alongside natural law.

etymology: From Greek deka logoi (ten words); the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:1-17; Deuteronomy 5:6-21). The Reformed-confessional tradition expounds the Decalogue as the summary of the moral law, with each commandment containing broad positive and negative duties drawn out by the rules of catechetical exposition (Westminster Larger Catechism Q. 91-152).
biblical_def: From Greek deka logoi (ten words); the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:1-17; Deuteronomy 5:6-21), the summary of the moral law given by God to Israel at Sinai and written by His own finger on two tables of stone (Exodus 31:18; 34:1). The Reformed-confessional tradition expounds the Decalogue as the perpetually-binding summary of the moral law, structured in two tables (the first table, commandments 1-4, governing duties toward God; the second table, commandments 5-10, governing duties toward neighbor; summarized by Christ in the two great commandments, Matthew 22:37-40). The Reformed exposition (especially the Westminster Larger Catechism Q. 91-152) draws out the broad content of each commandment by substantive rules of interpretation: (1) each negative commandment forbids the sin named and requires the contrary duty (the prohibition of murder requires the preservation of life); (2) each positive commandment requires the duty named and forbids the contrary sin; (3) each commandment governs not only the outward act but the inward heart, words, and thoughts (the Lord Jesus's exposition in the Sermon on the Mount, Matthew 5:21-48, drawing out the heart-level demands of the commandments against murder and adultery); (4) each commandment, under its species, comprehends all of the same kind (the prohibition of one sin includes all sins of that category, with their causes, means, occasions, and appearances). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Reformed exposition of the Decalogue as the comprehensive summary of the moral law, governing the whole of the Christian life in heart, word, and deed. The Decalogue is not abrogated (it is the moral law, perpetually binding) but is the rule of the believer's grateful obedience (the third use), expounded broadly to govern the whole range of moral duty toward God and neighbor.

webster_full: DECALOGUE (EXPOSITION), n. etymology: From Greek anti (against) + nomos (law); the theological error that denies the abiding obligation of the moral law in the believer's life. Various forms: doctrinal antinomianism (the law has no place in the believer's life), practical antinomianism (lawless living), and the historic antinomian controversies of the Reformation and Puritan eras.
biblical_def: From Greek anti (against) + nomos (law); the theological error that denies the abiding obligation of the moral law in the believer's life. The error takes several forms. (1) Doctrinal antinomianism: the position that the moral law has no place in the believer's life, that the believer freed from the law's condemnation is also freed from the law's direction (denying the third use of the law); various historic antinomians held that the believer is so united to Christ and so justified by grace that the moral law is no longer his rule of life. (2) Practical antinomianism: lawless living, the abuse of grace as license for sin (the error Paul addresses in Romans 6:1, shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?, answered God forbid). (3) The historic antinomian controversies: the Reformation-era controversy between Luther and Johann Agricola; the English antinomian controversy of the seventeenth century; the New England antinomian controversy involving Anne Hutchinson (1636-1638); and various recurrences. The Reformed-confessional response holds: justification is by grace alone through faith alone apart from works (against legalism), but the moral law continues as the rule of the justified believer's grateful obedience (against antinomianism); the grace that justifies also sanctifies, producing obedience to the moral law as the fruit (not the ground) of salvation. The substantive distinction: the believer is freed from the law as a covenant of works (he is not justified by law-keeping and is not condemned by the law) but not freed from the law as a rule of life (the moral law remains his rule of grateful obedience, the third use). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine against antinomianism: the grace of the gospel does not abolish the moral law but establishes it (Romans 3:31, do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea, we establish the law); the believer, freed from the law's condemnation, delights in the law as the rule of his grateful obedience (Psalm 119; Romans 7:22). The contemporary forms of antinomianism (hyper-grace, easy-believism, the cheap-grace gospel) are substantive errors the patriarchal-Reformed reader opposes.

webster_full: ANTINOMIANISM (DOCTRINE), n. (theological error; Greek anti [against] + nomos [law]) The error denying the abiding obligation of the moral law in the believer's life. Forms: (1) doctrinal antinomianism (the moral law has no place; the believer freed from condemnation is freed from direction; denying the third use); (2) practical antinomianism (lawless living, grace abused as license, Romans 6:1); (3) historic controversies (Luther-Agricola; English antinomian controversy; New England Anne Hutchinson 1636-1638). Reformed response: justification by grace alone apart from works (against legalism), but the moral law continues as the rule of grateful obedience (against antinomianism). The believer is freed from the law as a covenant of works but not as a rule of life. We establish the law (Romans 3:31). Contemporary forms: hyper-grace, easy-believism, cheap grace.

corruption_paragraphs: Antinomianism is the substantive error that denies the abiding obligation of the moral law in the believer's life, and it is opposed by the Reformed-confessional doctrine of the third use of the law. The antinomian holds that the believer, freed from the law's condemnation by justification, is also freed from the law's direction; he treats the moral law as wholly negative (only condemning, never guiding) and denies that the moral law is the rule of the believer's life. The Reformed-confessional response holds the substantive balance: justification is by grace alone through faith alone apart from the works of the law (against legalism, which would make justification depend on law-keeping); but the moral law continues as the rule of the justified believer's grateful obedience (against antinomianism, which would abolish the law's direction). The grace that justifies also sanctifies; the same gospel that frees the believer from the law's condemnation produces in him, by the Spirit, the obedience to the moral law that is the fruit (not the ground) of his salvation. Paul answers the antinomian abuse of grace sharply: shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid (Romans 6:1-2); and he affirms that faith does not make void the law but establishes it (Romans 3:31). John makes obedience the test of genuine knowledge of God (1 John 2:3-4). The patriarchal-Reformed reader opposes the contemporary forms of antinomianism (hyper-grace, easy-believism, the cheap-grace gospel that severs justification from sanctification and treats the moral law as irrelevant to the believer); the gospel of free grace produces, not lawlessness, but the Spirit-empowered obedience of the grateful believer who delights in the law of God (Psalm 119; Romans 7:22).

etymology: From Greek neos (new) + nomos (law); the theological error that the gospel is a new law requiring faith and evangelical obedience as the condition of justification, in place of the perfect obedience required by the original law. The opposite error to antinomianism; associated with Richard Baxter and the seventeenth-century English controversy.
biblical_def: From Greek neos (new) + nomos (law); the theological error that the gospel is a new law (a nova lex) requiring faith and evangelical obedience (sincere though imperfect obedience) as the condition of justification, in place of the perfect obedience required by the original moral law. Neonomianism is the opposite error to antinomianism: where antinomianism denies the abiding obligation of the law, neonomianism makes a softened version of law-keeping the condition of justification. The error was associated principally with Richard Baxter (1615-1691) and the broader seventeenth-century English controversy (the neonomian-antinomian controversy involving Baxter, the Baxterians, and their critics). The Baxterian / neonomian scheme holds: Christ's death altered the terms of the law, so that God now accepts faith-and-sincere-evangelical-obedience (rather than perfect obedience) as the condition of justification; the believer is justified not by Christ's imputed righteousness received through faith but by his own faith-and-evangelical-obedience reckoned as the new-law righteousness. The Reformed-confessional response rejects neonomianism as a substantive compromise of justification by faith alone. The grounds for rejection: (1) justification is by the imputed righteousness of Christ, not by the believer's own faith-and-obedience reckoned as righteousness (Romans 4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9); (2) faith is the instrument of justification (the empty hand that receives Christ's righteousness), not the condition or ground of justification (faith justifies not as a meritorious act of obedience to a new law but as the receiving instrument of Christ's imputed righteousness); (3) making evangelical obedience a condition of justification confuses justification with sanctification and re-introduces a works-principle into the gospel. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Reformed doctrine against neonomianism: justification is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, on the basis of Christ's imputed righteousness, with faith functioning as the receiving instrument (not the meritorious condition); the gospel is not a new law to be obeyed for justification but the proclamation of the free gift of Christ's righteousness. Neonomianism and antinomianism are the twin errors that the Reformed doctrine of justification holds between: against antinomianism, the moral law continues as the rule of the believer's grateful obedience; against neonomianism, justification is by Christ's imputed righteousness received through faith alone, not by the believer's own evangelical obedience reckoned as new-law righteousness.
